extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers and students interested in the history and social effects of gambling
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-historical survey of gambling across ancient and early-modern societies, tracing its prevalence, moral consequences, political uses, and social/economic effects. The text uses anecdotes, legal evidence, and classical authorities to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal prohibitions as evidence of a vice's existence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient to determine the existence of any special vice in a nation to find that there are severe laws prohibiting and punishing its practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text uses Egyptian law and its severe penalties (convicted gamblers sent to work in the quarries) as proof that gambling was prevalent; the presence and severity of legislation is treated as a reliable index of a vice's prevalence and the rulers' horror of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gambling used as an instrument of cruelty and political vengeance
rubrics_metrics.description: Gambling can be made subservient to the purposes of cruelty and murder (illustrated by Queen Parysatis, who played for the life or death of a slave).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotal evidence (Plutarch's account of Parysatis) is adduced to show how games of chance were used to determine life-and-death outcomes and to carry out political vengeance; anecdotes function as moral exempla demonstrating extreme consequences of gambling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/ethical distinction between games of chance and games of skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Muslims (here, modern Persians) argue that games dependent on 'skill' in management (as opposed to pure chance) are not prohibited, likening them to chess which is allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage reports the evasions used to reconcile gambling with religious prohibition: claiming skill rather than chance, and donating winnings as alms to avoid the appearance of playing for money. This distinction is presented as a common justificatory rubric in assessing permissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gambling undermines civic virtue and facilitates political subjugation
rubrics_metrics.description: The spread of gambling contributes to the decline of public spirit and aided Philip of Macedon's conquest — Athenians 'forgot all public spirit in their continued habits of gaming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical interpretation treats widespread gaming as weakening collective political resolve: examples include Greek civic neglect at Chaeronea and Aristotle's and Demosthenes' condemnations; the causal relation (dissipation → political weakness) is used as an evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral condemnation: gamblers equated with thieves and plunderers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities like Aristotle rank gamblers 'with thieves and plunderers, who for the sake of gain do not scruple to despoil their best friends.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical moral judgments are cited to characterize gamblers as socially depraved; such condemnations serve as a normative criterion when assessing the ethical status of gambling and gamblers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destructive escalation in certain games (doubling stakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Games in which the losers go on doubling their stakes resemble ever-recurring wars, terminating only with the extinction of the combatants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callistratus's remark is used as an analytical metaphor: particular betting systems (e.g., progressive doubling) are identified as structurally liable to ruinous escalation — a technical criterion for judging a game's destructiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheating as an inherent feature of gambling
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheating is a natural, if not a necessary, incident of gambling; evidenced by 'cogged' or loaded dice (Herculaneum) and historical instances of cheats being patronized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of cheating (loaded dice, organized deceit) is treated as an expected consequence of gambling culture; historical finds and anecdotes are marshalled to show how cheating corrodes trust and requires vigilance or legal response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gambling as a route to preferment and social advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of gaming or prominence at the gaming table could secure preferment or advancement (e.g., Vitellius, courtiers obtaining favour through play).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats gaming not only as vice but as an institutionally consequential practice that could alter careers and patronage; this criterion evaluates the political/social function of gambling within elite circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and social ruin resulting from gambling
rubrics_metrics.description: Gambling produced incalculable social affliction: ruinous debts, usury, lawsuits, and the destruction of families and fortunes (numerous historical examples cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses memoirs and anecdotes (lost fortunes of nobles, gaming academies' ruin) to argue that gambling causes systemic economic harms; the extent of lost sums and ensuing social consequences are treated as empirical measures of gambling's damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypocrisy and uneven enforcement of anti-gambling laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Although stringent laws against gaming existed and were revived (e.g., in France), the great and powerful continued to gamble, magistrates sometimes accepted bribes, and enforcement was selective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A gap between law and practice is presented as a diagnostic feature of a society's moral and administrative state; selective enforcement and elite exemption are used to evaluate the seriousness and effectiveness of prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalization and commercialization of gambling
rubrics_metrics.description: Gambling became institutionalized (Gaming Academies, licensed gaming houses) and commercialized (rooms hired by the hour, large rents paid, keepers profiting enormously).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The growth of gaming as a commercial enterprise — rental of rooms, organized salons, 'keepers' making large profits — is treated as evidence of gambling's social penetration and as a metric of its scale and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers and ministers using gambling to manipulate public sentiment or politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Political actors (Augustus, Mazarin, Henry IV) used gaming to flatter, distract, or further political designs (e.g., Mazarin induced the royal family to play to normalize card-playing at court).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text adduces examples where gambling was intentionally promoted or used by elites as a tool of governance or social control; such cases are treated as evidence of deliberate political manipulation via entertainments.
